system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: ocsf_enriched holds all three clouds normalized to the OCSF API Activity schema (one row per audit event; metadata.uid is the audit event ID), with context already joined onto every row in the `enrichment` struct: the person behind each principal (name, department, out-of-office, usual client OS and mismatch), service-account ownership and whether it called from outside its expected network, source IP reputation, asset classification, and for pod creates whether the workload is privileged, platform-allowlisted and from an approved registry. Tools search and summarize it directly; query_sql is available for anything else.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

input.summary: This alert is a real attack. Jordan Doe's (jdoe) credentials were used from 198.51.100.23, a known-malicious bulletproof VPS in the Netherlands (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING, tagged k8s_api_bruteforce and open_docker_registry:5000). Jordan is on PTO 2026-10-12..19 and normally uses macOS, but this client was Linux kubectl. The attacker ran the same playbook in order on EKS (14:02-14:25), GKE (14:38-15:01) and AKS (15:11-15:34). Steps: (1) checked their own permissions and listed namespaces; (2) tried to read kube-system secrets and create a kube-system job, and was denied; (3) read payments-db-credentials; (4) created a privileged alpine pod 'debug-tools-7f9c' with hostPID and the node's root filesystem mounted, then used exec with nsenter to get a root shell on the node; (5) used the node shell to steal the argocd-application-controller service account token (cluster-admin) and called the API with it from the same outside IP, which the Platform team's SA is not expected to do. With it they created ClusterRoleBinding 'jdoe-break-glass', giving jdoe cluster-admin. (6) With those rights they set up persistence: DaemonSet kube-system/kube-metrics-agent and CronJob kube-system/node-cert-rotate, both pulling images from the attacker's own registry at 198.51.100.23:5000, plus NodePort service default/metrics-agent-np on port 30080. (7) Finally they listed every secret in the cluster (the alerting event and its GKE/AKS equivalents). All three payments-prod clusters (PCI) are fully compromised. Every secret in each cluster should be treated as exposed.
